title: How To Handle Annoying Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses students who repeatedly approach with unimportant observations, suggestions, or tattles that aren't disruptive or rule-breaking but wear on a teacher's limited time. Rather than brushing them off, he recommends a three-step response: fully listen with genuine attention, respond briefly and honestly before thanking the student, and follow through visibly on anything promised. He argues that validating these small approaches, counterintuitively, reduces their frequency over time because the student's underlying need to be seen and heard is satisfied. He frames these interactions as a low-cost opportunity to build connection and rapport, cautioning that dismissing them risks damaging the relationship for the sake of only a few seconds saved.
points: Recommends fully listening to seemingly trivial student observations, suggestions, or tattles rather than brushing them off.
Advises a brief, honest response followed by a thank-you to close the interaction efficiently.
Stresses following through visibly on anything promised, even giving students a follow-up update.
Argues that validating these small approaches counterintuitively reduces their frequency over time.
Frames these brief interactions as a low-cost opportunity to build genuine connection and rapport.
quotes: They’re not interrupting or being rude. Nor are they breaking any rules. But it gets on your last nerve.
The best response, however, isn’t to shoo them away or tell them to mind their own business. No, the best response is to give them exactly what they want.
Although it may go against your every impulse, lean in and hear them out. Place your hand on your chin, look them in the eye, and take their concerns seriously.
If you embrace the concerns students bring to you, and validate them with your response, it tends to happen less often, not more.
It’s also their way of making a connection with you. It’s a moment you share together, pulling in the same direction.
So don’t mess it up. Don’t send them away, cut them off in annoyance, or risk sullying your relationship. Instead, welcome their thoughts. It takes just a few extra seconds of your time.
